meta.label: fictional
meta.note: Authored fictional world for the Standfolk demo. Every club, person, ground, and honour is invented. Statistics are generated from this file by scripts/world/generate.mjs and are fictional.
meta.national_team_note: National-team caps, goals, and careers abroad are fictional records about fictional people. Countries are real; no real league, club, or player is named.

history.text: Ferry crews found the club on Vellmouth's harbour wall.
First league meeting with Kestrin Athletic, the start of the estuary derby.
Quayside Park opens, facing the water.
The old harbour bell is moved into the north stand.
Second league title, won on the final day.
Third Brenmoor Cup, beating Hallowfield United in the final.

culture.title: The tide-bell song
culture.text: After each home goal the north stand rings the old harbour bell three times, then sings a slow harbour song.

culture.title: Ferry flags
culture.text: Supporters wave small blue-green signal flags, copied from the ferry crews who founded the club.

culture.title: The harbour walk
culture.text: Home fans walk along the harbour wall to the ground before kick-off.

fan_language.meaning: Said after a home goal, when the north stand rings the bell.
The club's nickname; also what fans call themselves.
The harbour-side stand behind the south goal.
Any league match against Kestrin Athletic.

history.text: Mill workers on the south bank of the estuary found the club.
First league meeting with Vellmouth Rovers.
Second Brenmoor Cup, the club's last major honour.
Supporters begin the wing salute as the team comes out.

culture.title: The wing salute
culture.text: Supporters raise both arms like wings as the team walks out.

culture.title: The Nest
culture.text: The covered terrace at Millbank Road where the loudest home fans stand.

culture.title: Shift whistle
culture.text: A mill whistle sounds at kick-off, a nod to the shift changes of the founders.

fan_language.meaning: Call for the wing salute; also said when Kestrin attack.
The home terrace at Millbank Road.
Kestrin's side of the estuary, and its supporters.

league_glossary.meaning: A match in which a team concedes no goals.
Two goals by one player in a match.
Three goals by one player in a match.
A match between close rivals in the table, where the result swings the gap twice.
The bottom three places; those clubs drop to the Brenmoor Championship.
A player who came through the club's own youth system.
A period playing for another club before returning.

England.background: The modern rules of football were first written down in England in 1863. Most professional players come through club academies.

Scotland.background: Scotland and England played the first official international match in 1872.

Wales.background: The Football Association of Wales, founded in 1876, is one of the oldest national football associations.

Northern Ireland.background: Northern Ireland's football association traces back to the Irish Football Association, founded in 1880.

Ireland.background: In Ireland football shares the stage with Gaelic games, and many players move abroad young to join academies.

Czechia.background: Czechoslovakia, which included today’s Czechia, won the European Championship in 1976.

Slovakia.background: Slovakia has had its own national team since 1993, when Czechoslovakia split.

Israel.background: Israel has played in Europe’s confederation, UEFA, since the 1990s, so its clubs and national team meet European opponents.

France.background: France has won the World Cup twice, in 1998 and 2018, and its national youth development system is widely studied.

Morocco.background: In 2022 Morocco became the first African team to reach a World Cup semi-final.

Japan.background: Japan’s professional league began in 1993. Many players come through school and university football as well as club academies.

Uruguay.background: Uruguay, a country of under four million people, won the first World Cup in 1930 and won again in 1950.

Ghana.background: Ghana reached the World Cup quarter-finals in 2010 and has a strong record at youth tournaments.

Netherlands.background: The Netherlands is known for “total football”, the fluid style of the 1970s, and for academies that stress technique.

Spain.background: Spain won the World Cup in 2010 and the European Championship in 2008, 2012, and 2024.

Denmark.background: Denmark won the European Championship in 1992 after entering late as a replacement team.

Argentina.background: Argentina has won the World Cup three times, most recently in 2022.

Nigeria.background: Nigeria won the Olympic football gold medal in 1996.

Hungary.background: Hungary’s “Golden Team” of the early 1950s reached the 1954 World Cup final.

Belgium.background: Belgium finished third at the 2018 World Cup.

Norway.background: Norway’s top division runs from spring to autumn, so transfers to other leagues often happen in the northern winter.

Sweden.background: Sweden’s top division also runs from spring to autumn. Sweden finished third at the 1994 World Cup.

Portugal.background: Portugal won the European Championship in 2016.

Croatia.background: Croatia reached the World Cup final in 2018 and finished third in 2022.

Poland.background: Poland finished third at the World Cup in 1974 and in 1982.

Finland.background: Finland reached its first major tournament at the European Championship held in 2021.

Korea Republic.background: South Korea reached the World Cup semi-finals in 2002, when it co-hosted the tournament with Japan. Many players come through school and university football.
